title: Wales 20 mph Casualty Attribution Audit: Companion Manuscript
oneLine: The paper behind the August 2026 Wales 20 mph audit: the 28% first-year fall reproduces as a description, but the published totals identify neither the size nor the sign of the policy's effect on the roads that changed.
abstract: Companion manuscript to the Evidence Press evidence package of 11 August 2026 (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21894035), which was released without a paper. On 17 September 2023 the default speed limit on restricted roads in Wales fell from 30 mph to 20 mph, and a provisional Welsh Government release reported that casualties on roads recorded as 20 or 30 mph were 28% lower in 2023 Q4 to 2024 Q3 than in the preceding four quarters. Using the package's corpus of 25 registered sources frozen on 11 August 2026, the manuscript reproduces the headline as a description (2,402 to 1,725 casualties, exactly -33850/1201 per cent) and reports that later frozen vintages give about -26.10% and -24.18%. It separates that statistic from the registered causal estimand, the effect on police-recorded casualties on road segments whose limit actually changed, and gives a constructive witness: three hypothetical worlds reproduce the observed aggregates yet imply effects of -50%, 0% and +100%. Within the frozen evidence and admitted rival set neither the effect nor its sign is identified, and no empirical bound is registered. The manuscript adds no new empirical analysis and does not change the package. It does not show that the policy succeeded or failed.
keyResults: The provisional first-year comparison reconstructs to 2,402 and 1,725 casualties on roads recorded as 20 or 30 mph, an exact change of -33850/1201 per cent (about -28.18%); later frozen vintages give about -26.10% (StatsWales) and -24.18% (DfT collision rows).
The published statistic covers every road recorded as 20 or 30 mph; the registered estimand is the effect on segments whose limit actually changed, relative to their unobserved no-policy outcome.

Three hypothetical worlds share the observed totals and the same affected/other split yet imply affected-road effects of -50%, 0% and +100%: neither the effect nor its sign is identified, and the values are not estimates or bounds.
Diagnostics (an England comparison whose pre-period differential reverses sign, outcome-scope sensitivity, speed-limit coding corrections) do not restore identification.
evidence: A 16-page manuscript with source, figure script, an AI-assisted adversarial review record with dispositions, and producer rerun logs of the evidence package's validation, citation, replay, table, test and lifecycle checks on 12 October 2026. The scientific records are those of the evidence package (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21894035), which this release does not change.
statusDetail: Unrefereed candidate. Companion manuscript reporting the frozen records of the 11 August 2026 evidence package without new empirical analysis. Producer-side replay passes; the review on record is internal AI-assisted adversarial review. No independent rerun, independent reimplementation, formal verification, external specialist review or editorial peer review has been established. The positive 28% attribution remains unsupported; no policy effect is estimated.
openProblems: Freeze a versioned historical segment map of roads that changed, kept 30 mph or later reverted, and link collision locations to it.
Specify and independently review a comparison design with several pre-period diagnostics, placebo dates and explicit anticipation and interference assumptions.
Independently reconstruct the source-vintage ladder and reimplement the observation-map witness without producer code.

narration:
In September 2023 Wales lowered the default limit on most roads that had been 30 miles per hour to 20. A provisional government release later said that casualties on roads recorded as 20 or 30 miles per hour were 28 percent lower in the first year than in the year before. This release asks whether that fall can be credited to the policy.

In August, Evidence Press published an evidence package auditing that reading, but without a paper. This release is the companion manuscript. It adds no new data analysis; it sets out the argument in full.

The 28 percent figure does reproduce: 2,402 casualties before and 1,725 after. Later official versions of the same comparison give smaller falls, about 26 and 24 percent. But the figure answers a different question from the causal one. It counts every road recorded at 20 or 30, including roads that never changed. And nobody observes what would have happened on the changed roads without the policy.

The manuscript makes that gap exact. It describes three imaginary worlds that produce the same published totals, yet in which the policy cut casualties on changed roads by half, did nothing, or doubled them. Because all three fit the data, the published totals cannot tell us the size of the effect, or even its direction.

That does not mean the policy failed, or that it worked. It means a causal answer needs different evidence: a historical map of which roads changed, linked to where collisions happened, and a defensible comparison.

This unrefereed candidate was released on the twelfth of October, twenty twenty-six. The manuscript, review record and the original evidence package are linked on the page. This synthetic briefing is not additional evidence.
